body: I'm tagging @TokageItLab because they wrote all of this code, so they can explain the intended meaning of the values exactly, and hopefully confirm that the limits are meant to be applied on the rest offset, not the incoming pose.

Please clarify. This is not a bug, it is just that the terminology used in the code is a bit confusing, right?

Since the code refers to the "pose when IK is not enabled" as "rest" as the resting state in IK, and call the result calculated by IK a “pose”, I think it is true that the variable name is not clear, but I do not think the algorithm itself is incorrect.

IK uses the forward vector calculated from "rest position (origin)" (or "pose position (origin)" when `mutable_bone_axis` is enabled), and the JointLimitation is based on this forward vector. In other words, we use either “rest” or "pose" for position depends on `mutable_bone_axis`, and we always use “pose” for rotation (so `mutable_bone_axis` affects only the calculation of the forward axis), then I am not sure what that mixture should be called, but in any case, there is no doubt that the pose should be used for calculating rotation.

Otherwise, it will completely ignore the results of the immediately preceding modifier or animation, and the moment IK is enabled, the root bone will reset from its current pose to the rest. If you want to ignore that, it should be easy for the user to intentionally disable a specific animation track or set the bone rest to bone pose by `reset_bone_pose()` or `reset_bone_poses()`.

Also, the reason we retain our own IK pose here is that, especially when the `Deterministic` option is disabled, this would result in a loss of continuity with the results from the previous frame. When `Deterministic` is enabled, the latest pose should always be reflected.

---

If you're referring to issues with ragdolls in PhysicalBone, that's a separate issue. Since the PhysicalBone code was implemented a long time ago and behaves internally like a rigid body. Since directly changing the rigid body’s position from the outside would break synchronization with the position and inertia data within the PhysicalServer, it is currently not possible to modify it externally.

See also https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_rigidbody3d.html#description :
> RigidBody3D implements full 3D physics. It cannot be controlled directly, instead, you must apply forces to it (gravity, impulses, etc.), and the physics simulation will calculate the resulting movement, rotation, react to collisions, and affect other physics bodies in its path.

So If you want to make PhysicalBone controllable with FK/IK, a fundamental change to the way PhysicalBone with respect to the PhysicalServer would be necessary.

Let me describe my current setup:
A custom body is created using rigid bodies and `Generic6DOFJoint3D` which perfectly align to the skeleton at rest. IK works as expected, the simulation can track the IK well enough when the bone poses are not updated by my modifier beforehand.

1. Custom modifier writes the joint rotations of `Generic6DOFJoint3D` to the skeleton pose
2. IK takes that pose as input and outputs a target pose
3. The custom modifier listens to the IKModifier3D `modification_processed` signal and updates the `Generic6DOFJoint3D` motors.
4. Physics space steps, back to step 1.

So to alleviate your concerns, I am using forces and I am certain that the motors are outputting the correct values. The problem I see is when I start writing the physically simulated result back to the skeleton pose, the limitations configured by me are applied on top of the incoming pose by CCDIK3D, so over time the smallest error caused by gravity slumps everything and sometimes joint rotations even invert as the IK appears to basically ignore any limitations. There is no "snap" and it breaks the limitation, the bodies are moving at fractions of millimeters per second, instead it just falls past the limitations very slowly, and then sometimes joints invert to keep the IK target, clearly showing the limitations are just not being respected.

With that out of the way, I was suspicious of these two codes pieces:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f08e003ff23a667c24c76c0193ba31a02b5dae99/scene/3d/ccd_ik_3d.cpp#L67
and
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f08e003ff23a667c24c76c0193ba31a02b5dae99/scene/3d/iterate_ik_3d.h#L167-L168

I interpreted this as the limitation being applied relative to the current pose, which would explain what I am seeing, which means it is only accurate in the editor while the skeleton is at rest, and when the skeleton is in rest pose just before CCDIK3D solves. If the incoming pose moves the bone slightly down, like the motor just sitting hundredths of a degree lower due to gravity, the limitation will now behave as if that was the rest pose, slowly moving that limitation as if it wasn't there at all.

There's also this documentation in regards to `mutable_bone_axes`:
> If `true`, the solver retrieves the bone axis from the bone pose every frame.
> If `false`, the solver retrieves the bone axis from the bone rest and caches it, which increases performance slightly, but position changes in the bone pose made before processing this **IKModifier3D** are ignored.

I have actually turned this to `false`, and the IK still happily solves from the incoming pose each frame, despite the documentation saying it would have ignored the incoming pose. Unfortunately, I have the special case where it must not reinterpret the bone axis from incoming modifiers, and apply limitations according to the bone's rest pose (which is how they would have been configured by users), but also start from the current bone poses and solve from there.

My initial suggestion may not be the solution, I've been trying to fix this at the source for a few days now and only just found this point as the possible bug. However, just calculating the global rest relative to the parent pose seems to not work, the IK is going wild now. I'll share my solution as soon as I find it.

If `mutable_bone_axes` is disabled, changes to the position will be ignored; however, if the length has been modified, the length calculations will not be synchronized, causing the IK to break. This becomes clear when you change the pose postion in the editor with gizmo enabled as you can see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111815. If you have modified the pose position beforehand, it is recommended that `mutable_bone_axes` be enabled.

And, when you say that limitations are ignored, does that mean the IKModifier ignores the Generic6DOFJoint3D? None of the SkeletonModifiers treat the Generic6DOFJoint3D as a limitation in the process. Instead, Generic6DOFJoint3D limitations are enforced by the PhysicalServer before or after modifiers application. Since the IKModifier has its own JointLimitation, you need to use that instead.

What I am saying is that the limitations I set on IterateIK3D appear to be ineffective if the incoming pose is not the rest pose, as it applies the limitations relative to the incoming pose. This means that for that iteration group, it will limit to, for example, 10 degrees on the X axis. Then it receives on the next frame the pose has moved 10 degrees, then it applies that limit on-top of the 10 degrees of motion, so now the limitation is 10 degrees from that new pose. This renders the limit to basically be a glorified "max angular delta" if the pose on the skeleton is not the rest pose. Does this make sense?

And, I have no angle limits on the Generic6DOFJoint3D for the axes that the IK is free to rotate on, I hope to have the joints "break" if they stray too far beyond the limits I configured from the IK settings. For example, the IK is only free on the X axis, but is restricted to 10 degrees. Then the Generic joints are constrained on YZ, but have no constraint for X. But, because those IK setting limits always apply relative to the incoming pose, they basically mean nothing anymore.

I'm still trying to find the solution in the code, I am currently convinced that CCDIK3D applies limits always relative to the incoming pose, meaning they only work if that incoming pose is the normal skeleton's rest pose.

First of all, are you using JointLimitation? The “max angular delta” value indicates the maximum angle that can be moved in a single iteration; it is by no means a limitation. This is also stated in the documentation.

Yes that is what I was trying to say, that I am using that limitation and it is applied relative to the incoming pose when I believe it should be applied relative to the local rest pose transformed by the parent bone's global pose.

The result is that when the IK is fed back it's resulting pose output, it turns that limitation into a glorified "max angular delta", so that there really is no overall limitation being applied anyway. I mentioned it to make it clear that limitation is behaving the same way as max angular delta.

Ah, I see. It is true that currently, limitations are applied depending on the pose direction. This is because in some cases, IK axis limitations are performed based on the state after posing.

For example, there are cases where the IKRoot is pointed toward a secondary target using an AimModifier before IK, allowing the secondary target to be used like a PoleVector, see also [this example](https://godotengine.org/article/inverse-kinematics-returns-to-godot-4-6/#tweak-boneconstraint3d). JointLimitation also needs to follow this, but the particular problem here is that the Gizmo does not match the internal behavior. This is a bug.

There might be cases where one wants to use rest only for limitations, but as mentioned above, since there is a reason why the current behavior is necessary, that would be an enhancement. Implementing this is not very difficult; it is just a matter of passing the original rest to `get_projected/limited_rotation()` or `get_rotation/limitation_axis_vector()`. However, since SpringBone also has the same options, it would need to be applied there as well.

> Ah, I see. It is true that currently, limitations are applied depending on the pose direction. This is because in some cases, IK axis limitations are performed based on the state after posing.

I think this is what the bool `mutable_bone_axes` is meant to do. As it stands, bones are effectively always mutable with CCDIK3D regardless of what the value of the bool is. I'm thinking my original suggestion is the way it should be, grest and lrest should really be initialized to the actual rest poses of the bones, unless mutable is enabled, then it should read the incoming pose and operate with that.

Update on my end: I changed this line and now my problems seem to be gone. Technically the IK had always worked before because the `grest` and `lrest` rotations were actually the true rest poses, so just making them stick to that makes the limitations work without the bones suddenly going wild.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f08e003ff23a667c24c76c0193ba31a02b5dae99/scene/3d/iterate_ik_3d.h#L167
changed to use `get_bone_rest` instead.

It might work in your case, but it’s not correct because it discards all previous transformations even when there are no limitations; Unless the axis is fixed, we must keep the bone twist before IK. As mentioned above, I don’t think it makes much difference from calling `reset_bone_pose()` manually, so I don’t see the point. So at least, you should only call it when the axis is locked, and in cases where the axis is not locked and only Limitation is enabled, a different approach will likely be necessary.

> It might work in your case, but it’s not correct because it discards all previous transformations even when there are no limitations. As mentioned above, I don’t think it makes much difference from calling `reset_bone_pose()` manually, so I don’t see the point.

I do need the IK to solve from the incoming poses, but so far this was the smallest change that respects the limitations. I'll update again when I get both working.

UPDATE: enabling `deterministic` happens to force a copy of the global bone poses into the working chain for IterateIK3D. For now I'm satisfied with my hacks, but I hope this problem can be reasonably simply fixed. Everything I tried to be more precise in the limitation fixes just caused the joints to seem to ignore them even more and sometimes instantly snap into wild poses.
